country.comment: The study analyzes a socio-environmental water conflict in Alajuela province, Costa Rica, specifically involving the canton of Atenas and the district of Tacares in the canton of Grecia.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1 (Title, Resumen, Abstract); PDF p. 3, Section 1; PDF pp. 7-8, Section 3

effect_estimate.comment: Qualitative case study reconstructing a ~7-8 year socio-environmental water conflict (2012-2019); secondary descriptive statistics on Atenas population (25,460), 2014 daily water rationing prevalence (60%, citing Fornaguera 2014), project cost (2,800 million colones), and tank storage (2,500 m3) are cited as context on PDF p. 3, with no quantitative inferential effect estimate.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Unplanned real-estate growth without municipal regulatory/land-use plans left Atenas canton with severe water shortages (60% of its 25,460 inhabitants facing daily water rationing in 2014), prompting the national water utility (AyA) to launch a top-down inter-basin water transfer project from Parque Recreativo Municipal Los Chorros in Tacares in December 2012 without prior community consultation. Tacares residents mobilized and filed legal remedies (a constitutional recurso de amparo and annulment of environmental viability) that paralyzed and delayed the works. Two subsequent negotiation phases—direct negotiation via the Comisión Técnica Negociadora (2013-2014, whose preliminary agreement failed community assembly ratification) and facilitation by the Defensoría de los Habitantes—reproduced power asymmetries, promoted participation only reactively after conflict escalated, failed to reach consensus, and ended with AyA completing the project in 2019 as originally designed without incorporating negotiated alternatives (though the conflict spurred creation of AyA's Unidad de Gestión Social y Participación Ciudadana in 2014).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1 (Resumen, Abstract); PDF p. 3, Section 1; PDF pp. 7-12, Section 3; PDF pp. 13-15, Section 4

mechanism_certainty.comment: Primary qualitative case study (appraised with CASP Qualitative Checklist; design ceiling = 2) that directly documents—through semi-structured interviews with community negotiators and AyA's executive president, institutional minutes, and media records—how top-down project design without participation, judicial injunctions (recurso de amparo and environmental viability nullification), and two-stage institutional negotiations operated on the multi-year delay and eventual completion of the Atenas water supply project.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 3-4, Section 1; PDF pp. 10-12, Section 3; PDF pp. 14-15, Section 4

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines unplanned urban expansion without regulatory/land-use plans or urban containment boundaries (planning, zoning), park land-tenure issues in negotiation agendas (tenure), multi-year project paralysis and construction delay (delay), community exclusion vs. negotiated consultation and creation of AyA's social participation unit (participation), leadership-dependent bureaucratic openness under AyA's executive presidency (discretion), inter-municipal/state-community coordination across Atenas, Grecia/Tacares, ASADA de Tacares, and AyA (political_coordination), constitutional injunction and environmental-viability annulment halting works (judicial_review), and Ombudsman facilitation via Defensoría de los Habitantes (complaint).

outcome_flags.comment: Analyzes community water access and supply deficits in Atenas alongside protection of future water supply for Tacares (water_access), lack of permanent water supply and daily rationing affecting 60% of Atenas residents in 2014 (service_continuity), water flow/volume diversion and 2,500 m3 storage expansion to meet growing urban demand (service_quantity), and paralysis/7-8 year delay in completing the water supply infrastructure project from 2012 to 2019 (delay).

study_design.comment: Operationalized using three stages of Alpízar's (2013) Modelo de la Espiral del Poder y el Ciclo de las Demandas Políticas (construction/destruction, articulation/disarticulation, and institutional processing of political demands) and Acselrad, Das Neves & Muñoz's (2010) negotiated conflict-resolution typology.
study_design.value: Qualitative case study (semi-structured interviews with local community and institutional actors, plus documentary review of institutional minutes and local/national media reports)
